methodological_rigor.justification: The study uses multiple complementary systems, including public human GBM single-cell RNA-seq, murine glioma, breast cancer, melanoma, chronic LCMV infection, TNFR2-knockout mice, adoptive transfer, flow cytometry, bulk RNA-seq, CD8 depletion, pharmacologic TNFR2 antagonism, anti-PD-1 combinations, intracranial and subcutaneous tumor models, and rechallenge experiments. Cell-line authentication elements such as mycoplasma negativity, detailed tissue processing, antibody information, and repeated experiments are reported. Statistical methods are generally appropriate, including t tests, ANOVA, regression, log-rank tests, and multiplicity correction for survival comparisons, but the manuscript does not describe randomization, blinded outcome assessment, formal power calculations, or full handling of all repeated-measure and sequencing multiplicity issues.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: This is a mechanistic preclinical study using mouse tumor and chronic viral infection models plus reanalysis of human single-cell data, so Oxford level 5 applies. The work is translationally relevant because T-cell exhaustion limits checkpoint blockade response and TNFR2 antagonism plus anti-PD-1 improved tumor control, including intracranial glioma models. Clinical relevance remains indirect because no patient treatment cohort or human functional validation of TNFR2 blockade is presented.

reporting_quality.justification: ARRIVE is the most applicable standard for the animal experiments. The manuscript reports mouse strains, age ranges, tumor implantation procedures, humane endpoints, tissue processing, antibody doses, statistical tests, sample sizes in figure captions for key therapeutic experiments, and public accession sources for reanalyzed single-cell data. Reproducibility is moderate because custom scripts and public datasets are referenced, but raw experimental RNA-seq/flow data, randomization/blinding details, and full protocols are not completely available in the normalized text.

novelty_literature.justification: The paper advances a novel mechanistic link in which TNFR2 upregulation precedes TOX expression and promotes progression toward terminal T-cell exhaustion. TNF, TOX, and checkpoint-resistance biology are well established, but the proposed TNFR2-upstream-of-TOX model and the PD-1 plus TNFR2 antagonist therapeutic experiments across multiple tumor compartments are a substantial conceptual and translational extension. The novelty is somewhat limited by reliance on preclinical systems and previously recognized interest in TNFR2 as an immunotherapy target.

writing_presentation.justification: The manuscript is clearly organized and builds a coherent mechanistic sequence from human and murine single-cell observations to functional phenotyping, knockout studies, transcriptomics, and therapeutic antagonism. Methods are unusually detailed for animal handling, flow cytometry, tumor implantation, viral qPCR, sequencing, and statistical analysis, and figure captions provide sample sizes and test choices for key experiments. The article is dense and occasionally uses strong mechanistic language where causality is still partly inferred from knockout and antagonist models.

key_strengths: Strong mechanistic arc connecting TNFR2 expression, TOX regulation, exhaustion transcriptional programs, and antitumor immunity.
Findings are tested across human single-cell data, several murine tumor models, chronic LCMV infection, knockout mice, adoptive transfer, CD8 depletion, RNA-seq, and pharmacologic antagonism.
Combination TNFR2 antagonism and PD-1 blockade improved tumor control and survival in both subcutaneous and intracranial models.
Detailed methods and figure captions support evaluation of experimental reproducibility.
key_concerns: No patient-level therapeutic validation of TNFR2 antagonism is included.
Randomization, blinding, and formal power calculations are not clearly reported for animal experiments.
TNFR2 is expressed on several immune and nonimmune cell types, so antagonist mechanisms may not be fully T-cell intrinsic.
Direct epigenetic validation of the proposed TOX-associated reprogramming is deferred to future work.
chief_reviewer.rationale: This is a strong preclinical immuno-oncology manuscript with broad model validation and a plausible therapeutic strategy; minor revisions should mainly temper causal claims and clarify animal-study rigor.
